# This MiniCluster manifest is designed to run the Kripke benchmark on a single AWS ARM-based Kubernetes node.
# It is configured for a CPU-based instance and specifies the ARM architecture for the Flux container.
# The job is set to run a single pod (size: 1) but will execute the command across 4 tasks within that pod.
# It also includes resource requests for AWS EFA networking, which is common in HPC environments on AWS.
apiVersion: flux-framework.org/v1alpha2
kind: MiniCluster
metadata:
  # Using a unique name to avoid collisions in the default namespace.
  name: kripke-minicluster-1
  namespace: default
spec:
  # The total number of pods to deploy for the MiniCluster.
  # Set to 1 to run the entire job on a single node as requested.
  size: 1

  # The total number of MPI tasks to run. These tasks will be distributed
  # among the pods defined by 'size'. Here, all 4 tasks run in the single pod.
  tasks: 4

  # Keep pods and services around after the job finishes for debugging.
  cleanup: false

  # Enable strict validation for the MiniCluster spec.
  logging:
    strict: true

  # Defines the main application container that will be orchestrated by Flux.
  containers:
    - image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/fractale-agent-experiments:kripke
      # The command to execute, which will be wrapped by `flux run`.
      # Kripke is run with no additional parameters.
      command: kripke
      # This container is not the lead broker/launcher pod; it's a worker pod.
      # This setting MUST be false.
      launcher: false

  # Flux-specific configuration.
  flux:
    # Specify the architecture for the flux-view container image.
    # This is required for ARM-based instances like AWS Graviton.
    arch: "arm"
    container:
      # Use the ARM-compatible version of the flux-view container.
      image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/flux-view-rocky:arm-9

  # Pod-specific configurations that apply to all pods in the MiniCluster.
  pod:
    resources:
      # Requesting AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) for high-performance networking.
      # This is crucial for HPC workloads on AWS to achieve low latency and high bandwidth.
      limits:
        vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1"
      requests:
        vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1"

# This corrected MiniCluster manifest addresses the previous validation error by moving the resource
# definitions to the correct location within the container spec.
# It is configured to run the Kripke benchmark on a single AWS ARM node, utilizing 64 tasks
# to leverage the node's full CPU capacity. It includes EFA-specific environment variables
# and Flux options for performance, as suggested by the expert review.
apiVersion: flux-framework.org/v1alpha2
kind: MiniCluster
metadata:
  # Using a new name to avoid collision with the previous attempt.
  name: kripke-minicluster-2
  namespace: default
spec:
  # The total number of pods to deploy for the MiniCluster.
  # Set to 1 to run the entire job on a single node.
  size: 1

  # The total number of MPI tasks. This is set to a higher value to utilize
  # the full capacity of a multi-core CPU instance.
  tasks: 64

  # Defines the main application container orchestrated by Flux.
  containers:
    - image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/fractale-agent-experiments:kripke
      # The command to execute. Per instructions, Kripke is run with no parameters.
      command: kripke
      # This container is a worker, not the launcher. This MUST be false.
      launcher: false
      # Resource requests and limits MUST be defined on the container, not the pod spec.
      # This section is moved here to fix the "unknown field" error.
      resources:
        limits:
          vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1"
        requests:
          vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1"
      # Environment variables required for EFA to function correctly.
      environment:
        FI_PROVIDER: efa
        FI_EFA_USE_DEVICE_RDMA: "1"
        LD_LIBRARY_PATH: /usr/lib64

  # Keep pods and services after the job for debugging purposes.
  cleanup: false

  # Enable strict validation of the MiniCluster specification.
  logging:
    strict: true

  # Flux-specific configuration.
  flux:
    # Specify the architecture for the flux-view container image for ARM instances.
    arch: "arm"
    # An additional Flux option to ensure each task is pinned to a specific CPU core.
    optionFlags: "-o cpu-affinity=per-task"
    container:
      # Use the ARM-compatible version of the flux-view container.
      image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/flux-view-rocky:arm-9

  # Pod-specific configurations that apply to all pods in the MiniCluster.
  pod:
    # A restart policy of "Never" is appropriate for batch jobs.
    restartPolicy: Never

      # Environment variables required for EFA to function correctly.
      environment:
        FI_PROVIDER: efa
        FI_EFA_USE_DEVICE_RDMA: "1"
        LD_LIBRARY_PATH: /usr/lib64

  # Keep pods and services after the job for debugging.
  cleanup: false

  # Enable strict validation of the MiniCluster spec.
  logging:
    strict: true

  # Flux-specific configuration.
  flux:
    # Specify the architecture is ARM for the flux-view container.
    arch: "arm"
    # An additional Flux option to pin each task to a specific CPU for performance.
    optionFlags: "-o cpu-affinity=per-task"

      # Use the ARM-compatible version of the flux-view container.

As described in literature such as 'Kripke: A Massively Parallel Transport Mini-App' (LLNL-TR-658712), these codes are often communication-bound. In a strong scaling scenario, the fixed total problem size is divided among an increasing number of processors. This leads to a smaller computational workload per processor, which can cause communication overhead to dominate the total runtime and limit scalability. This study will proceed to collect data to observe this expected behavior and determine the point at which scaling efficiency degrades.

As described in the Kripke user manual and performance reports like 'Kripke: A Massively Parallel Transport Mini-App' (LLNL-TR-658712), this leads to a smaller computational domain per processor. Consequently, the surface-to-volume ratio increases, meaning the proportion of time spent on communication (surface) versus computation (volume) grows. The observed performance drop indicates that for this problem size, the cost of communication between the two nodes outweighs the benefit of halving the computational work per process. The application has hit its strong scaling limit immediately.

This suggests that the problem size is too small to overcome the network communication latency and overhead introduced when distributing the work across multiple nodes. For this configuration, Kripke is communication-bound and does not scale beyond a single node.
